summary:
Alaska falls in the Moderate-Risk group of Erin In The Morning's July 2026 legal-risk assessment, alongside Kentucky and North Carolina. That tier is defined as states that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. It sits above the assessment's worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below its protective groupings.

No statewide statute bars a transgender adult from using a public restroom or changing room matching their gender identity, and no statewide law bans gender-affirming care for adults. Pressure has reached Alaska through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. Gov. Mike Dunleavy's earlier attempt to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while boards he appoints have restricted transgender girls' participation in girls' sports.

The State Medical Board, whose members Dunleavy appoints, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation that would classify providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as unprofessional conduct, exposing clinicians to disciplinary action. A board member had proposed the resolution in June 2025. The draft must be vetted by the Alaska Department of Law and then pass a 30-day public comment period before it can take effect.

The Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 in September 2023 to bar transgender students from female sports and athletics statewide. Facilities policy below that level is set district by district. The Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex assigned at birth or a private alternative such as the nurse's office, replacing guidance that had stood for more than seven years; the policy was described at the time as an apparent first for Alaska. It binds one district's schools and does not extend to adult facilities anywhere in the state.

Alaska's statewide nondiscrimination law does not cover gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order protecting state employees from discrimination addresses sexual orientation only. Four municipalities, Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, home to about 46% of the state's population, prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing. Ketchikan's ordinance passed unanimously in July 2020 and took effect in mid-August 2020. Anchorage's ordinance passed 9-2 in September 2015 and survived a repeal attempt on 3 April 2018, when voters rejected Proposition 1 by 53% to 47%; that measure would have required people in public spaces to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their sex assigned at birth. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly.

Alaska's hate-crime statute does not list gender identity, so bias-driven violence against a transgender person does not trigger a state-level penalty enhancement. A visitor outside the four municipalities with local ordinances has no state or municipal recourse against discrimination in a hotel, restaurant or workplace.

Document changes are available and leave a record. An amended Alaska birth certificate with a corrected name and gender marker requires a Birth Certificate Request Form, a photocopy of identification, a letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus a fee. The amended certificate keeps the previous legal name printed at the bottom with a notation that it was originally issued under the former name and amended because of a change of name. Changing the gender marker on an Alaska driver's licence requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment, or an already-updated birth certificate or a court order for gender change.

Marriage licences have issued without regard to the sex of the spouses since 13 October 2014, after the federal district court in Hamby v. Parnell struck down the state's statutory and constitutional bans; the statutory ban had been allowed to become law without Gov. Tony Knowles' signature in 1996, and a constitutional amendment passed on 3 November 1998. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry in Alaska.

Private consensual sex between adults is not criminalised. Alaska repealed its sodomy law with effect from 1 January 1980; the 1899 statute had punished the crime against nature with up to ten years in prison.
tangentialFactors:
The State Medical Board's August 2025 agenda carried a statement opposing late-term abortion alongside the resolution on gender dysphoria in minors, placing two unrelated policy questions before the same appointed body in one vote.

Because the youth-care and school-sports restrictions move through appointed boards rather than floor votes, the operative rules can shift with board membership and with the governor who fills the seats, without a legislative session.

Alaska's constraint on adult visitors is thin by statute and heavier at the regulatory edge; the measures that materially affect a visiting adult are document rules, the absence of statewide nondiscrimination coverage, and the hate-crime gap, not a prohibition on adult care or adult facility use.

National measures that bind travellers across the United States are carried by the national assessment for the United States, not by this state record.
localsOnly:
Residents outside Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan have no state or municipal protection against gender-identity discrimination in private employment, housing or public accommodations. State employees rely on a 2002 executive order that names sexual orientation only, leaving gender identity uncovered in state employment as well.

Clinicians and families in Alaska face the draft regulation approved by the State Medical Board on 22 August 2025, which would make providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 unprofessional conduct and open providers to discipline. Until the Department of Law review and the 30-day comment period run their course, the board's action is a recommendation plus a draft, not an operative rule.

Family law recognises married couples as adoptive parents. A non-genetic, non-gestational mother is treated as the legal parent of a child born through donor insemination only where the parents are married. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation, and while Alaska has no surrogacy statute, courts have generally been favourable to surrogacy arrangements.

Anchorage banned conversion therapy on minors in August 2020 by a 9-2 vote, the first such municipal ban in Alaska.

Students in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough School District attend school under the October 2022 rule requiring bathrooms matching sex assigned at birth or a private alternative; the policy applies to that district only.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the State Medical Board's August 2025 recommendation has been formally adopted, and the final text of the draft regulation after Department of Law review and public comment, are unresolved.

No inventory material records enforcement of the four municipal nondiscrimination ordinances in gender-identity complaints, so the practical reach of those protections is not sourced.

The inventory holds no count of trans-specific violence in Alaska and no general homicide rate for the state, so no comparison between the two can be made.

Whether school districts beyond Matanuska-Susitna have adopted similar facilities policies is not sourced, and the full reach of the September 2023 Board of Education sports rule across district athletics programmes is not itemised.

Whether Alaska law enforcement has issued guidance on investigating bias crimes against transgender residents is not in the inventory.
